item.title: Filicide Is a Societal Problem
item.description:
Postpartum Depression

Filicide Is a Societal Problem

Our society needs more resources for parents.

Posted October 29, 2026

Key points
  • Postpartum depression/psychosis is only one part of the problem when we talk about infanticide.
  • We leave mothers in particular and parents in general alone to do a very difficult job.
  • Before a mother breaks down, she needs help and support.

Recently, The New Yorker published an article about filicide. It focused on one case in particular—and it was not the case of Lindsey Clancy. This was the case of Nakira Griner, a New Jersey mother accused of killing her toddler in 2022.

I would like to make three points regarding these two cases—and the many others like them that occur with frightening regularity.

1. Color matters.

One of the points made in the article is that the media attention has been on Clancy rather than Griner.

Clancy is white. Griner is Black.

2. Interpretation matters.

When a white middle-class mother murders her children, we tend to talk about mental health. When a Black mother from an impoverished background is accused of killing her toddler, we tend to talk about murder.

This is important—and, obviously, egregiously unfair.

In both cases, a crime was committed. And in both cases, it is likely that psychosis played an important part. And when it comes to filicide, as is true with many brutal crimes, it is hard to know where to draw the line between severe mental illness and criminality.

3. These deaths have to do not just with the difficulties of diagnosing postpartum psychosis but also with the failure of our society to support parents and families.

The deaths of these children occurred within a specific context—and that is the context of a society in which parents are left completely alone to fend for themselves.

In the United States in particular, and in the developed world in general, more parents live farther away from and are more cut off from their families of origin than ever before in history. And being a parent, and especially, in many cases, being a mother, is not a job that should or can be done alone.

A great deal of research has been done by sociologists and anthropologists demonstrating that human primates require community support in infant and child rearing. For example, anthropologist Sarah Blaffer Hrdy writes that humans are cooperative breeders, meaning that mothers have historically relied on a network of helpers to raise infants. She calls these helpers “allomothers” and defines them as group members such as grandmothers, older siblings, aunts, uncles, fathers, and non-kin allies who actively help hold, watch, and feed infants.

So, where are the allomothers these days?

In what we sometimes call “primitive” societies as well as in many countries where traditional family groups are maintained, allomothers are still available. But in our country, as in most developed nations, this is not the case.

Most mothers in developed nations either have no helpers or they have very few—and those helpers who do present themselves often have very limited availability. And these same helpers are there to take care of the infants or children, not to help the mother herself or to provide for her needs.

Overview

The fact is that postpartum depression and/or psychosis do need to be paid more attention to; psychiatrists, psychologists, social workers, primary care physicians, police detectives, lawyers, etc. do need to be trained to recognize postpartum psychosis and to find appropriate treatment for mothers experiencing this condition. More light does need to be shed on this problem, and more education does need to be provided not only to the professionals who might be involved but also to the general public.

But postpartum depression/psychosis is only one part of the problem when we talk about infanticide.

Clancy was very ill. Griner was very ill. And, crucially, they were also alone. For hours and hours each day.

As it turns out, Clancy had been ill for quite some time, but apparently no one knew exactly how psychotic she had become.

Griner was not just ill; she had also been severely abused and neglected as a child and was being abused as an adult.

No one knew all the details of either of these women’s inner lives.

As any parent knows, spending hour upon hour with infants and children is difficult, sometimes tedious, and occasionally infuriating. When a mother’s stability is tenuous, whether due to a life of abuse and neglect or a current period of disordered thinking, the strains of parenting can become overwhelming and impulses usually kept in check can be difficult to control.

And we must ask ourselves what we can do to help mothers in these situations before they or their impulse control breaks down.

As a society, we alternate between idealizing all the wonderful mothers out there (sometimes including our own) and knowing that mothers have frailties and foibles and need help and support.

We know that mothers need someone to trade off with. They need someone—an allomother perhaps—to give them a break, to hold or feed their babies, to give them time to eat a meal. But more than that, we know that mothers need companionship while they mother; they need others with whom to compare notes and share responsibilities—and they need someone, perhaps a number of someones, to make sure they are OK, and to provide for some of their needs.

But we do very little to see that our society provides for these needs.

And what’s more, I suspect that the media seized on the Clancy story not only because, of course, we all love some drama in our lives, as well as a bit of schadenfreude, but also because we are all living in a time and a place where we, to one degree or another, feel quite abandoned by our society, and in particular by our government as well. On some level, we cannot imagine being Clancy or Griner….but on another level, we can. As parents, we may feel rage with our children; we mostly do not act on it, but at those moments we may feel alone in our parenting and our personhood.

And these days many of us feel quite alone in our lives in a society and in a time that does not prioritize social support, relatedness, or connection, all things desperately needed by mothers—as well as by the rest of us.

A version of this post also appears on the Thoughtful Parenting website.

item.title: Start Close In
item.description:
Mindfulness

Start Close In

Personal Perspective: What I discovered from feeling without naming.

Posted October 29, 2026

Something happens in my chest. There is a tightening, a little pressure, a sensation I don’t like. Within seconds, I have identified the problem: It is anxiety. Or perhaps frustration. Maybe it’s envy, which would explain why it arrived just as I was reading about somebody else’s six-figure book deal.

Lately, I’ve noticed how quickly I try to explain a sensation to myself. Something happens, and before I’ve had much chance to feel it, I’m telling myself what it is, why it’s there, and what I should do about it.

Then last week, a Ukrainian word made me wonder what might happen if I waited a little longer before giving a sensation a name.

Alexandra Shunrun
Source: Used with permission/Alexandra Shunrun

A Word for the Uncomfortable Middle

On my podcast, Fifty Words for Snow, my cohost Emily John Garcés and I explore words that don’t have easy English equivalents. This week our guest Alexandra Shunrun introduced us to nezruchno, a Ukrainian word that describes something uncomfortable, inconvenient, or awkward.

Alex explained that a meeting time could be nezruchno if it didn’t fit your schedule. A pair of shoes could be nezruchno if they pinched your feet. You might feel nezruchno asking someone for a favor or admitting that you’d forgotten their name. You could also feel nezruchno if you failed to do something you’d promised someone.

If I failed to keep a promise, I would probably say I felt guilty. But Alex described a more complicated experience: feeling empathy for the person you let down, feeling stress about an upcoming confrontation, and perhaps also feeling uncomfortable with yourself for being a person who let someone down. The feelings might overlap, and it might be hard to sort out exactly what you were experiencing.

My co-host Emily wondered whether we sometimes reach for the word “guilt” because it seems close to the feeling, even when we don’t necessarily feel we’ve done anything wrong. Maybe a friend asks for a favor and I feel a little twist in my stomach, so I say yes, because I think the twist is guilt. Later, I realize I didn’t have time to do the favor, and what I felt might have actually been reluctance. Or I wanted to help but was worried I’d disappoint her. Or maybe all of those things were true.

I liked that nezruchno could leave room for the tangle. I can recognize that I’m uncomfortable and feel the physical components of it without immediately deciding what category of emotion to put it in. In English, I can say I feel uneasy, unsettled, awkward, or simply uncomfortable. But nezruchno brought my attention to how much can be happening inside that “ugh” before I’ve settled on an explanation.

Start Close In

In my Buddhist group, we’ve talked about paying attention to how feelings show up in the body before we get conceptual about them. Recently, I’ve been giving it a real try. When I notice a knot in my stomach or tightness in my jaw, I pause before deciding I’m angry or anxious. I ask myself: What does this sensation actually feel like? Is it pressure? Heat? Does it stay in one place or move around? Does it have edges? And if I notice that I don’t want to feel it, I get curious about that, too. What does not wanting feel like in my body?

My teacher, Sylvia, describes what she calls the apprehending mind, “the mind that closes down around something and then grasps it, solidifies it, then embellishes it into a storyline.” The trouble, she says, is that we then respond to what we’ve made up: We create the world, we react to our creation as if it were solid, and our thoughts proliferate.

I recognize this process. My chest tightens while I’m reading about someone else’s book deal. I call it envy. Then I think about my most recent book, which is out on submission. Then I begin to wonder why I haven’t heard from the publishers. Within minutes, I’m imagining that no one will ever want the book and I will be forced to condemn the manuscript to the bottom left-hand drawer of my desk, the designated purgatory for all of my dead projects. By the time I’m thinking about the fate of my book and the dead project drawer, I’ve traveled a long way from the original sensation of tightness in my chest.

Recently I’ve been trying to short-circuit the process. As I do, I’m discovering how impatient I am, how I want to immediately label any discomfort I encounter, find its cause, and then get rid of it. I start to wonder about all the times my body was trying to communicate something and I interrupted, attempting to manage it with a diagnosis.

Sylvia is clear that the practice isn’t to treat conceptualization as the enemy: “Our thoughts are not bad. They are just part of a natural process.” The mind, she says, is just doing what it does. So instead of forcing the thoughts away, we notice them and gently interrupt their momentum. “We don’t hit it over the head and say, ‘Stop,’” she says. Instead, we say, “Just a minute.”

Sometimes I think of the opening of David Whyte’s poem "Start Close In":

Start close in/don’t take the second step or the third/start with the first thing/close in…

For me that first thing is the physical sensations that appear before a storyline develops.

I don’t mean that we should never name our feelings. Knowing that I’m angry can help me recognize that a boundary has been crossed. Knowing that I’m sad can help me ask for comfort. And sometimes a physical symptom calls for a doctor, not an extended session of somatic experiencing. But I’ve noticed that a name can feel so definitive and solid that I check out once I’ve landed on it. I call something anxiety and straightaway move on to manipulating it, without noticing the subtleties of the feeling, its changing nature, or whether there might be something else mixed in.

Sylvia talks about inviting the mind to come home to the body, where there’s a different sort of wisdom, a sort of warm nourishing psychic hearth, a place where language holds no sway.

Staying with Nezruchno

After talking for a bit on our podcast episode, Alex began second-guessing how she would use the word nezruchno in her own language. The more closely we examined it, the harder it became to pin down. I found that impressive: Even the person who brought us the word, a native speaker who had used it all her life, was willing to sit with a little uncertainty about it.

I still like an explanation. If my chest tightens, I will probably continue to interview the usual suspects. But now, once in a while, I can say: Something feels nezruchno. Let me see what happens next.

item.title: Is It Onboarding or Hazing?
item.description:
Workplace Dynamics

Is It Onboarding or Hazing?

What separates normal new-job discomfort from humiliating tests?

Posted October 29, 2026

Key points
  • Workplace hazing can be disguised as onboarding, banter, or team socialisation.
  • When newcomers are humiliated, they don't ask questions and don't seek support.
  • Belief in the tradition and team dynamics often perpetuates hazing.

"Can you get us 12 coffees? Fresh into a new job, and told to go out and get everyone coffee. "I don't have a list; you're on your own." Or, "As a junior nurse, Lisa took a difficult patient on her second shift with no handover and no backup. When she asked for help, she was told to 'toughen up'." Everyone nods. That's the way it is here.

Companies dismiss these experiences as a tradition that newcomers go through; however, it is hazing. Studies focusing on the treatment of new employees reveal that hazing is much more common than most people believe. Somewhere between a quarter and three-quarters of American workers say they have experienced hazing at work.

What counts as hazing?

Bullying is often associated with hazing, but they are not the same. Bullying can happen to anyone, whereas hazing is what we put the newcomer through. Hazing is when we make a newcomer do an undesirable task or take part in a humiliating or coercive process (Thomas, Cimino, and Meglich, 2021).

Starting a new job is often uncomfortable. Research on organizational socialization finds that some discomfort is expected for a new employee. However, hazing has three features that distinguish it:

  1. It doesn't teach anything. Getting coffee for 12 people doesn't make a person better at the job. Being left alone with a difficult patient on the second shift doesn't either. It's not about skill. And nobody cares if the individual can do the job. It's about testing if they will say yes without support.
  2. It has an audience. The whole point: Other people are watching. Being made to tell an embarrassing story in the lunchroom, being called out in front of the team in the coffee room. We show the "newbie" that they don't matter as much as we do.
  3. It is a power test. No one is checking if the newbie can do the work. Instead, the person is tested. Are they willing to accept unreasonable demands?

Once they have proven themselves, it usually stops. And that's what makes it so easy to brush off as just initiation.

Why do we let it continue?

We start to think it's normal. In 'system justification,' we would like to believe the way things are is the way things should be, even when it sucks for some people. It's easier to rationalise it than to challenge it. With hazing, we hear the same things: "We all went through it." "It's tradition." "It creates team bonding." "We have to earn our place."

How much "tradition" matters comes up in the research. According to Thomas and Meglich (2019), people were more likely to find hazing acceptable if it is an established tradition, especially in a close-knit team. Group cohesion is a main determinant of hazing acceptance. This helps explain why hazing can be difficult to eliminate.

People who accept it are accepted, and people who reject it leave the group. Over time, the practice is normalised and passed on to new members. In the attraction-selection-attrition theory, organizations select and retain individuals who fit existing norms and values, while those who do not fit are more likely to leave (Schneider, 1987).

People with higher authoritarian traits are more likely to haze; people who think that hierarchical relationships are desirable may believe that newcomers should "earn" their position in the group (Thomas and Meglich, 2019). This may provide some insight as to why some of those who have been hazed will go on to haze others. Those who have paid the price for admission may feel it is fair that others pay the price.

What it costs

Hazing is bad for business. As a newcomer, if you're concerned about being judged, you won't ask questions or want feedback. This is when you make mistakes. According to Ellis and colleagues (2015), newcomers assess workplace demands against the resources available to them. Negative experiences like humiliation, exclusion, role ambiguity, and lack of support draw away resources but provide no room for growth. That leads newcomers to have higher anxiety, lower job satisfaction, decreased organizational commitment, and increased intention to quit. It's not the job itself that causes this, but the lack of resources to cope with the additional stress.

That resource drain also messes with safety. If a junior nurse is too scared to say "I don't know how to do this," that's a real risk and a bad onboarding experience.

One recent study shows that when hazing is normalised, people start to rationalize other unethical actions. We think: This is how we do things." And it gets easier to excuse the next line being crossed.

How to stop hazing

Instead of managers letting the team run their own tests to see if someone belongs, give people a proper plan for the first four weeks. Check-ins that actually happen. The mentor who is never seen again after day one does not work: "Come to me if you need anything."

And watch out for this wording: "Earn your stripes." "Toughen up." "That's just how we do it here." We probably have a standard created. Tradition is not a good excuse to haze.

The first few weeks shape how someone sees an organisation for years. It's a simple question: Are we helping newcomers settle in, or making them earn the right to belong?

item.title: Better Together: The Power of Being Around Other People
item.description:
Social Life

Better Together: The Power of Being Around Other People

A new study investigated the positive effects of being around other people.

Posted October 29, 2026

Key points
  • Meaningful social interactions with family members and friends often increase positive emotions.
  • Not much had been known about how just spending time around other people affected emotions.
  • A new study investigated the association between time spent in the company of people and positive emotions.
  • Just being around other people was enough to boost happiness.

You may have heard the phrase “Misery loves company”, but psychological research has shown time and again that the reverse is true: Happiness loves company. Being in the company of other people and doing something fun together has been shown repeatedly to increase positive emotions and general psychological well-being. In contrast, being completely alone for a long time and having strong subjective feelings of loneliness leads to negative emotions in most people. What is less well understood, however, is how being around other people, but without interacting with them, affects emotions and psychological well-being.

How being around other people affects emotions in older adults

To close this major knowledge gap, a new study, just published in October 2026, was focused on understanding how spending time around other people, but without having any social interaction with them, affects positive emotions (Goldman & Moorman, 2026). Published in the journal Socius: Sociological Research for a Dynamic World, the study titled “Happiness Loves Company? Positive Affect and the Momentary Social Context” was based on an analysis of data from 352 older adults living in Chicago. The researchers used a method called ecological momentary assessment. Each volunteer who participated in the study was handed a smartphone and had to carry it around for three one-week periods, about five to six months apart. During those three one-week periods, volunteers were messaged five times each day to provide the scientists with information about what they were doing and how they felt.

To find out how the volunteers felt, the scientists asked them the following three questions:

  • Did you feel happy?
  • Did you feel content?
  • Did you feel energetic?

Volunteers also had to indicate whether they were all alone, or in the company of a family member, friend, romantic partner, pet, neighbor, or any other person. If a volunteer indicated that they were around other people, they then had to answer a few follow-up questions about whether they knew some or all of the other people around them. This way, the scientists could distinguish people in four different social states:

  • all alone
  • in the company of friends or family, but with no other people around
  • around people that they did not know, but with no friends or family members around
  • in the company of friends or family, and additionally, having other people around

Both socializing and just being around people increased happiness

Overall, the team analyzed more than 12,000 data points collected from the volunteers. Across all data points, the volunteers who participated in the study showed moderate levels of positive emotions. As was to be expected, people who were in the company of friends or family but with no other people around were happier than people who were all alone. But interestingly, volunteers who were around people that they did not know, with no friends or family members around, were also happier than people who were all alone. The highest level of positive emotions was observed in situations in which volunteers were simultaneously in the company of friends or family and that of other people they did not know.

Takeaway

Humans are social animals, and the results of this study make it clear that it is not only deep and meaningful social interactions with people we have known for ages that make us happy; sometimes just being around people in general gives a boost in happiness. These findings are especially important during a time when more people spend an increasing amount of time alone scrolling on their smartphones. Also, they highlight the importance of ensuring that older relatives and friends do not spend too much time all by themselves. So the next time you think about whether you should visit your grandma, do it!

item.title: What if Big Tech Is Actually Minimizing Risks to Humanity?
item.description:
Denial

What if Big Tech Is Actually Minimizing Risks to Humanity?

Decades as a psychologist have taught me the complex dangers of denial.

Posted October 29, 2026

Key points
  • AI researchers warn of human extinction, yet many dismiss their warnings as corporate hype.
  • Big Tech has powerful incentives to minimize existential risks, not exaggerate them.
  • Psychological defenses help us dismiss threats too frightening to contemplate.
Source: Image created with ChatGPT / OpenAI

We’ve been hearing from multiple people lately that there’s about a 10 percent chance that humanity will be extinct relatively soon because of artificial intelligence (AI).

And one of the popular and, for me, most perplexing responses to warnings like this? That Big Tech is exaggerating the danger to make itself richer and more powerful. The idea is that the handful of richest men who ever existed on this planet are so manipulative and eager for money that they are going to threaten us with death so that we give them even more power and they make even more money.

Wait…what?

Since When Is Killing Your Customers Good Marketing?

The argument is that portraying AI as extraordinarily dangerous will cause us to hand over even more power to them. This, in spite of the fact that many researchers over the years have verbalized the exact same argument with the exact opposite goal—that of motivating us to control Big Tech. It seems clear to me that acknowledging the potential destruction of humanity risks hurting Big Tech more than it could possibly help. But let’s consider the flip side of this argument, an alternative that IMO is more likely—that is, that it’s true that they are lying, and lying in a way that protects them, but it’s the opposite lie: They are minimizing the risk to humanity.

If anything, history gives us plenty of reasons to suspect that companies minimize dangers rather than exaggerate them; think Big Tobacco or Exxon. When enormous amounts of money are at stake, corporations have repeatedly downplayed risks to the general population. In fact, these Big Tech bros have already been found guilty in court of lying to us by minimizing the harms of AI, and owing consumers hundreds of millions to even billions of dollars. Yet, suddenly we trust them on the extinction bit?

It makes no sense to me that we rarely discuss the possibility that Big Tech is continuing to play by its playbook of understating the danger to humanity. Why assume these companies would suddenly change their approach on this one issue of extinction and tell us and their investors everything they really believe? To me, the much higher likelihood here is that they are minimizing the risk of human extinction.

Furthermore, we aren’t even talking about the possibility of civilization collapse. This is different from total extinction, and actually probably much more likely. Throughout history, human civilizations have collapsed, but some humans have lived on. Similarly, it seems that this possibility of civilization collapse would be even more likely than total extinction today. Most, but not all, humans dead? In fact, this issue was recently studied. A few months ago, MIT published a collaboration with the University of Queensland Psychology Department, surveying 272 AI specialists from 37 countries. The experts were asked to estimate the odds of a catastrophic outcome from AI in the next 5 years. Yes, you read that right: the next 5 years. (Catastrophic outcome was defined as more than one million deaths, more than $100 billion in financial losses, or comparable harms.) In sum, several risks were estimated at greater than 20 percent, while 18 of the 24 risks were estimated as at least 10 percent likely. Ultimately then, it may be more probable that we will experience the collapse of our civilization than total human extinction. So, if Big Tech is so motivated to be overestimating the risk of extinction, why are they literally ignoring the potentially even more likely possibility of civilization collapse?

I believe we owe it to our children, and our ancestors, to consider this.

Maybe We Just Don't Want to Believe It

Humans are extraordinarily skilled at self-deception. As one obvious example, we insist we’re independent thinkers while readily accepting the influence of people literally called influencers, whom we know are financially motivated to manipulate us into buying stuff. Psychologists have spent decades studying why humans are so adept at avoiding uncomfortable realities, and examples are many. Cognitive mechanisms like normalcy bias lead us to assume that because things have always worked out before, they'll continue to work out. Motivated reasoning supports our embracing explanations that allow us to feel safe and in control, even when we aren’t. Intellectualization lets us debate probabilities and motives rather than confront their implications. And when all else fails, there's always the most basic of defense mechanisms: denial. My guess is that our tendency toward denial is exactly what Big Tech is counting on, and so far, we haven’t disappointed them.

We've Seen This Movie Before

Literally. It's called Don't Look Up. In the film, scientists discover a comet heading toward Earth. Yet humans go to great lengths to minimize or simply ignore the threat. The disturbing part of that movie isn't the comet but how recognizable the human behavior is.

I’m coming to the conclusion that perhaps the most dangerous thing about AI isn't that we don't understand the warnings. It's that we understand them perfectly well and have become exceptionally good at explaining them away. But denial isn't inevitable, and if my years as a psychologist have taught me anything, it’s that denial generally leads nowhere good. Instead, owning our power and looking directly at what frightens us strikes me as our only realistic option. We can join together, demand answers, and insist that the future of humanity is far too important to leave in the hands of a few billionaires.

item.title: The Quiet Cruelty of Erasure
item.description:
Career

The Quiet Cruelty of Erasure

Rejection says you weren’t chosen. Erasure says you were never seen.

Posted October 29, 2026

Key points
  • Being treated as if you don't exist can wound more deeply than outright rejection.
  • Research on ostracism shows that being ignored activates brain regions linked to physical pain.
  • Self-erasure can begin as a survival skill and harden into a trap.

Theresa attended a town hall at work to hear the new VP and department head share his strategic vision for the coming year. When he put up the organizational chart, she noticed something was missing: her name. In fact, her entire team had been left off.

When it came time for Q&A, Theresa stood up and asked whether she should read anything into that omission about the organization's future strategic focus.

The VP simply said that her team was no longer lucrative.

His answer shocked Theresa, not for its brutal honesty, but because it dismissed everything her team had achieved over the years.

“It felt like the VP invited us to dinner and didn’t set a place for us at the table.”

What Theresa experienced is called erasure—the quieter cousin of rejection, and sometimes the more painful of the two.

Why erasure hurts more than rejection

Rejection tells you that you weren’t chosen. Erasure makes you wonder whether anyone ever saw you. Rejection at least confirms you exist. Being erased tells you your reality doesn’t count.

Social psychologist Kipling D. Williams spent his career studying ostracism, the experience of being ignored and excluded. One of his key contributions is Cyberball, a simple online ball-tossing game. A participant plays catch with two other “players” who, after a few throws, stop passing the ball to them.

It’s a trivial game played with strangers. Yet being left out reliably makes people feel hurt, angry, and diminished within minutes. Brain imaging studies using Cyberball found that social exclusion activates some of the same regions involved in processing physical pain. Our brains register being ignored as a kind of injury.

Williams found that ostracism threatens four basic needs: belonging, self-esteem, control, and a sense of meaning in our lives. People tend to respond in one of two ways. Some make desperate efforts to be seen, while others withdraw gradually. When exclusion persists long enough, many reach resignation: a state of alienation, helplessness, and a quiet conviction that they don't matter.

Erasure and shame

Erasure doesn’t only happen in conference rooms. For a child who is abused and then not believed, or a gay kid who never sees himself reflected in the world around him, the lesson is that the true self must stay hidden.

That’s toxic shame, almost by definition. Erasure teaches, “Something about me is unspeakable.”

When we erase ourselves

Erasure isn’t always imposed externally. Over time, many of us learn to do it to ourselves.

Self-erasure often begins as a survival skill and then becomes a trap. Hypervigilance, excessive people-pleasing, and numbing with alcohol or other substances can all be ways to make yourself smaller, so you’re less of a target. These strategies work in the short term but cost a great deal over time.

When institutions erase

Psychologist Jennifer Freyd coined the term “institutional betrayal” to describe what happens when an institution fails the very people who depend on it. When an organization minimizes or hides abuse, the survivor is harmed twice: first by the abuse and then by being written out of the record. Silence becomes policy.

I know this firsthand. When I finally told my parents my Scoutmaster was molesting me, they confronted the troop’s senior leaders, but were shamed into silence. Decades later, I was among more than 95,000 survivors who filed claims against the Boy Scouts of America. As part of the process, I was asked to complete a 47-page questionnaire recounting in detail my years of abuse.

The pattern is unmistakable: abuse, silence, and revictimization, all over again.

The antidote is witnessing

Being seen, named, and believed reverses erasure. That’s why testimony and support groups heal, not just inform. Telling the story puts a person back into the record

I can only speculate why the VP thought it was OK to omit Theresa and her team. He should have acknowledged the team's accomplishments instead of dismissing their value. At the very least, he owed them an apology for omitting them from the org chart.

By standing to ask her question, though, Theresa forced the VP’s hand and put herself back on the org chart. What eventually happened to her or her team is beside the point. What matters is that Theresa refused to shrink so someone with authority on stage could feel big.

item.title: 'The Animal Invitation' Celebrates Human-Animal Relations
item.description:
Ethics and Morality

'The Animal Invitation' Celebrates Human-Animal Relations

A timely and readable wide-ranging book by Paul Waldau.

Posted October 29, 2026

Key points
  • A must-read book for anybody who is interested in learning about and improving human-animal relations.
  • The author stresses the importance of people representing different fields and views talking with one another.
  • He smoothly weaves in science, stories, religion, and spirituality and offers a much needed pillar of hope.
  • The book stresses that every moment of every day each human lives and acts in a more-than-human world.
Source: Frans van Heerden/Pexels.

The study and nature of human-animal relationships is not only a "hot" area of interdisciplinary research by scholars representing many diverse areas, but also of great interest to numerous humans who "meet" nonhuman animals (animals) in a wide variety of contexts. Indeed, a scientific field of inquiry called anthrozoology focuses on the myriad ways we encounter animals and the various ways we interact with them.

For these and many other reasons, I am thrilled that one of anthrozoology's finest, the eclectic Dr. Paul Waldau's new book titled The Animal Invitation: Science, Ethics, Religion and Law in a More-than-Human World, is now available for consumption by people directly and indirectly interested in learning about and improving how we interact with a wide variety of animals ranging from household companions to wild neighbors to individuals of species most of us will never see up close and personal. On a personal note, Paul has been my mentor for many decades.

Marc Bekoff: Why did you write The Animal Invitation?

Paul Waldau: I wanted to memorialize the growth and development of my views while I directed two graduate programs that offered science-based degrees focused on animal protection issues. Teaching gifted students for several decades led me to recognize that any truly enlightening approach to “the animal question” must be multi-disciplinary. Such an approach produces dynamic learning not only in science but also in three other key areas—ethics, religion, and law. These insights prompted the subtitle Science, Ethics, Religion and Law in a More-Than-Human World.

MB: How does your book relate to your background and general areas of interest?

PW: The book allowed me to explore three important forces in my life: 1) a family background and daily life that constantly introduced me to nonhuman animals and cultural diversities. 2) insights available through working with other scholars and activists. 3) insights that emerge when one does a comparative study of religions, legal systems, science-based explorations, and moral and ethical traditions

MB: Who do you hope to reach?

PW: General readers who want to explore (i) their local world and (ii) the wider worlds so evident in diverse geographical locations affected by distinctive cultural heritages; activists who focus on (i) education; (ii) animal protection; or (iii) ecological issues; and educators who want to teach their students how to take charge of their own learning.

MB: What are some of the topics you consider, and what are some of your major messages?

PW: To explore the limits of educational approaches focused on a single discipline, I ask a series of basic questions about how much better we would educate future generations if we exposed students to essential ideas about animals from different disciplinary approaches. Below are four basic questions I ask in The Animal Invitation. Together, these questions show that tackling the animal question through a single discipline isolates the researcher and yields fewer insights than a multidisciplinary approach.

Question for those who study science: How much better would our scientific exploration be if, as we go about each of our many different science fields that in some way explore nonhuman animals, we already knew a great deal about (i) what our ethical systems have suggested about other animals, (ii) what our religious traditions have claimed, and (iii) what our legal systems have in the past done and now might attempt because they play such a prominent role in every modern nation-state?

Question for those who study ethics: What might we learn about ethics if, for the purpose of seeing this human capac­ity as well as possible, we search our human legal systems, our religious and wis­dom traditions, and our many sciences to fathom what humans can know of our nonhuman neighbors and our own animal features?

Question for those who study religious traditions: Can we better fathom our religious and wisdom-spirituality traditions if we have also noticed, taken seriously, and dispassionately explored the animal fea­tures evident in how humans have pursued and now in science, eth­ics, and law?

Source: Brill/with permission.

Question for those who study law: How much better will our species understand what different human communi­ties have attempted through the law if, as we attempt such an understanding, we have already explored our own animal features seriously as they connect us to what is claimed about nonhuman animals in our sciences, ethics, and religions?

MB: How does your work differ from others that are concerned with some of the same general topics?

PW: An interdisciplinary approach reveals not only key questions for everyone, but also:

  1. How narrow our discussions of ethics, of animal law, and of both social sciences and physical sciences will remain if they do not become interdisciplinary,
  2. How discussions of the history and present state of religious belief systems will fall far short if they concentrate solely on human matters
  3. How science-based discussions have historically remained narrow and unaware of key nonhuman animal insights that many of our predecessor human cultures have achieved regarding that each human life is irretrievably part of a more-than-human world that constitutes our larger community.

All of these insights are needed for humans to recognize that our own membership in the larger animal community is a key to each human’s full actualization.

MB: Are you hopeful that as people learn more about the importance of connecting with other animals, they will treat them with more respect, dignity, and compassion?

PW: I am hopeful for five reasons. First, the past half-century shows how humans can recognize both our own animality and our nonhuman kin among the Earth’s bountiful living communities.

Second, each of the four disciplines discussed gives us important reasons to engage fully with the fact that every human today lives, as did all our ancestors, irretrievably in a more-than-human world.

Third, spirituality in humans’ religious traditions can, with work, match the keen insights our indigenous ancestors, as well as those alive today in still-existing indigenous traditions, developed to guide both their local community and individuals.

Four, today’s legal systems, through the extraordinary expansion of animal law courses in law schools around the world, may soon provide increased awareness that our kind of living being can, if we choose (and as our ancient ancestors chose), use legal systems to honor the fact that the larger community of all living beings constitutes our greater self.

Finally, our remarkable physical and social sciences today have begun to engage beyond the species line in ways that confirm that human beings are by no means the only remarkable animals in the Earth community.

item.title: Analyzing the Concept of Unconscious Bias
item.description:
Unconscious

Analyzing the Concept of Unconscious Bias

If a bias is unconscious, then it is inaccessible to awareness.

Posted October 29, 2026

Key points
  • Consciousness is the foundation of human awareness.
  • Consciousness allows us to self-reflect and interact with the external world.
  • The unconscious refers to that which exists outside conscious awareness.
Source: Gerd Altmann / Pixabay

Consciousness is the foundation of human awareness. Through consciousness, we are able to think, reason, question, reflect, judge, choose, and acknowledge ourselves, others, and the external world.

Consciousness allows us to constantly and immutably self-reflect and interact with the external world. It also provides us with the conscious and intellectual capacity to recognize assumptions, beliefs, preferences, and values (Frith, 2023; Kriete, 2025): "I think, therefore I am" (Descartes), or, "I am what I think, do, say, learn and choose" (Purje, 2014).

What about the unconscious? The unconscious refers to that which exists outside conscious awareness. It is unknown to the conscious self.

Imagine being asked what lies behind a door in a house that is unknown to you. There is no meaningful answer because the object of inquiry is entirely unknown. In the same way, asking an individual to identify an “unconscious bias” presents the same paradox (Levy, 2017).

If a bias is unconscious, then it is inaccessible to awareness, and self-evidently, whatever this unknown entity is, it cannot be consciously directed, regulated, or evaluated by the individual (FitzGerald & Hurst, 2017).

The Essence of Conscious Awareness

The moment a person reflects upon a like, dislike, or preference—or identifies an assumption and examines a belief—that is when this “content” becomes a thought and enters the essence of conscious awareness (Greenwald & Krieger, 2006; Jolls & Sunstein, 2006; Levy, 2017).

As such, it becomes something that can be questioned, evaluated, supported, dismissed, and analyzed as many times as the individual so desires (Jolls & Sunstein, 2006; Levy, 2017).

Immanuel Kant argued that ethics and morality rest upon rational agency and so human beings are responsible for their actions because they possess the capacity to reason, analyze, deliberate, and make conscious choices. The Categorical Imperative assumes the existence of rational thought and conscious reflection. A person acts ethically and morally because they possess the ability to examine principles and determine whether those principles could be universally applied.

If ethics and morality depend upon conscious reasoning, an important question follows: How can a person be held accountable for something that is, by definition, unknown to conscious awareness? The universal answer is they cannot (Levy, 2017).

A proponent of “unconscious bias” may choose to say to another, "Your actions tell me that you are acting from unconscious bias." There is but one universal answer to this: “I don’t know what you are talking about.”

Free Will

Because of consciousness, we have free will, and because of this—as noted in Responsibility Theory—we are responsible for, and have power over, what we think, do, say, learn, and choose (Purje, 2014).

As such, we can choose to like or dislike anything and/or anyone. We can choose to agree or disagree with anyone and/or anything. We can choose to have an opinion, and we can choose to change that opinion, as many times and as often as we want. In the same way, we can choose to believe or disbelieve whatever we want. There is no limitation to this intellectual, conscious power.

Consequently, a person can choose to believe in the concept of “unconscious bias.” However, a belief in this concept does not make it a universal truth.

Source: Gerd Altmann / Pixabay

A Universal Truth Requires Objective Proof

From a Kantian perspective, a universal truth requires objective proof that satisfies human reason, not merely a subjective belief.

Kant would remind us that we cannot claim universal certainty about a concept that, by its very definition, completely evades conscious human experience. Therefore, any ethical or moral judgment or "rule" based on“unconscious bias” does not meet the test of the Categorical Imperative.

For a principle to meet this standard of universality, it must be an ethical and moral rule that a rational person can consciously choose to universally act upon without contradiction.

Because the Categorical Imperative demands deliberate, rational, and reasoned choice, "unconscious bias" cannot form the basis of any universal ethical or moral duty. Consequently, you cannot logically command a rational agent to be ethically or morally responsible for a concept dictated by something their own conscious mind cannot perceive.

item.title: Indices for Psychological Disaster Resilience
item.description:
Resilience

Indices for Psychological Disaster Resilience

A recent study researches Indonesian teenagers.

Posted October 29, 2026

Key points
  • The Student Social Resilience Scale for Disasters was developed and tested for Indonesia.
  • Psychological disaster resilience requires a combination of individual and community influences.
  • The process of completing the survey can support teenagers’ psychological disaster resilience.

Indices and scales are inevitably examined for mental health and psychological impacts of disasters. A recent effort looks at secondary school students in Indonesia.

A paper by four Indonesian researchers titled “Development and validation of the Student Social Resilience Scale for Disasters (SSRD) among adolescents in disaster-prone areas” was published in the journal BMC Psychology.

Detailing the research

The study’s sample comprised 800 randomly selected secondary school students aged 15 to 18, balanced by gender across Indonesia. They were given the Student Social Resilience Scale for Disasters comprising 28 statements which they had to rank on a Likert scale from 1 to 5.

The statements were adapted to be relevant for this study’s context and were translated into Indonesian, the official language of Indonesia. An example (in English) is the scale’s original statement of “My friends stand by me during difficult times” which became “My friends are always ready to help and be with me in emergencies”. Another example is altering “Spiritual beliefs are a source of strength for me” to “My spiritual beliefs are a source of strength in my daily life and give me the strength to face emergencies”.

The study sought to validate this particular scale, the Student Social Resilience Scale for Disasters, and it states that it did so. Of particular importance was adapting the original scale for disasters, demonstrating that such changes could and should be made to ensure that the scale becomes relevant for a particular topic. An additional aspect was confirming that no resilience in disaster situations is about the individual alone or only the social situation around the individual. Instead, personal, community, and contextual factors influence students’ disaster resilience in tandem.

Physical distancing for COVID-19 prevented disease spread while affecting psychological resilience.
Source: Ilan Kelman

Thinking beyond the study

One question is why the study focuses on “disaster-prone areas,” as stated in the title, the abstract, and throughout the paper. The paper’s location of Indonesia certainly has numerous disasters. This situation reflects the world: Everywhere is disaster-prone and disasters happen everywhere.

In fact, the paper uses the term natural disasters without critique, even though Indonesian disaster researchers have been world leaders in adopting the axiom from disaster science that disasters are not natural. Any school and any student in the world could be affected by the environment, whether it is a volcanic eruption grounding commercial flights across a continent as occurred for Europe in 2010, a drought leading to water restrictions across a city, or a vegetation fire making it difficult to breathe through the smoke and particles hundreds of kilometres away.

Plus, every school in the world was significantly affected by the COVID-19 pandemic from 2020-2023 and the measures to deal with this pandemic. Examples included the closure of schools and facilities, as well as students and staff isolating for days when they became ill. A study published last year in the journal Current Psychiatry Reports by two American authors detailed the mental health impacts of US students returning to the classroom after COVID-19-related closures.

The disaster-proneness of all schools is terribly demonstrated by shootings. 2026 has seen massacres in schools in the rural town of Tumbler Ridge, British Columbia, Canada, and in the capital city of Thailand, Bangkok. No place seems to be immune from this form of disaster.

Additionally, Likert scales have their place, but the known limitations must be acknowledged and overcome. Examples of long-documented difficulties with Likert scales include reliability and consistency of respondents alongside limitations of many statistical procedures to deal with the data.

Cultural biases can intrude. An implicit construction in a Likert scale is that the distance is the same between each choice of the scale. Different people and different cultures might view the distances between each number as different, depending on how the central option (often presumed to be neutral) is considered in comparison to less central numbers such as 1 and 5.

Lessons from the study

Yet no single study can cover all aspects, and this one provides important lessons to be applied elsewhere. The study is not just about the data, but is also about the process of collecting the data.

First, the authors make an excellent point that much other work examines only individual or only community aspects of resilience, no matter how “resilience” is defined. The power of the scale used here is that it brings them together and contextualises them. Second, the detail and specificity of the 28 statements ensure that respondents start considering the issues mentioned. Whether or not respondents tick the boxes consistently or robustly, asking them to think about statements such as “I am always open with my family or caregivers about my feelings and concerns” means that they might look at ways to better communicate “feelings and concerns” with their “family or caregivers”. They might then become more open.

Resilience is not merely a number determined by completing a survey. It is a process bringing together people, those around them, and their social and environmental contexts—exactly as the research here presents.

item.title: Humor on the Move
item.description:
Humor

Humor on the Move

Why travel comedies are perfectly designed to generate audience laughter.

Posted October 29, 2026

Key points
  • Travel comedies have been a staple of the film industry for more than a century.
  • They set up a need for characters to reach a destination, then incorporate dozens of elements to hamper them.
  • Highlighted physical, emotional, cognitive, and social vulnerabilities serve to inspire audience laughter.
Source: Ceren / Pexels

Readers familiar with this blog know that I have a thing for patterns that provide insight into why we laugh. One such pattern is the long-standing link between comedy and the act of traveling. There is something about getting into a vehicle—whether a car, bus, plane, train, or boat—and transporting oneself from A to B that seems conducive to feelings of amusement. What might explain this relationship?

As a point of reference, a list produced by the Internet Movie Database under the heading of “Road Trip Travel Comedy movies” provides more than two dozen examples, including National Lampoon’s Vacation, We’re the Millers, EuroTrip, Harold and Kumar Go to White Castle, Orange County, Miss Stevens, Going the Distance, and Away We Go. One could add as well the classic Planes, Trains, and Automobiles. Plenty of other comedies feature memorable travel-related scenes that get the audience laughing. Tommy Boy and Little Miss Sunshine come to mind.

Vulnerability in Motion

What’s going on? As an advocate of the Mutual Vulnerability Theory of Laughter, I have some thoughts. According to this worldview, the feeling of amusement is intimately tied to the perception of vulnerability. When we observe someone—especially those with whom we have some emotional connection—display a shortcoming, limitation, or frailty, we often communicate a sense of shared vulnerability with our laughter. By communicating that we too have had to overcome some of the same difficulties, we help lift their status (and hopefully their spirits). It provides solace. It helps designate us as potential cooperators. And for others who have displayed some arrogance or stupidity, reminding them they share the same limitations we do serves to lower their status and reestablish greater equality. Both messages tend to facilitate mutually beneficial cooperation in the future.

What we see time and time again in travel films are sympathetic characters displaying dozens of vulnerabilities audiences can easily relate to. These include certain character qualities and just plain bad luck that tend to make reaching their objectives more difficult (i.e., “shortcomings”), but still fall short of making it impossible (what would be interpreted as serious “deficiencies”).

Keep in mind that to determine what is and isn’t a vulnerability, the audience needs to be clear about what goal is being sought. For travel films, a big part of the goal is to reach the intended destination. That’s where the action is, or will be, that determines whether or not the hero or heroine (or with whomever a given audience member most identifies) will find some measure of success. In the travel film genre, we see a dozen or so recurring themes.

Source: Chris John / Pexels

Environmental Factors

What impedes people on the way to reaching their destination? Many factors are largely out of the control of the characters involved. These include things like mechanical breakdowns. There are a host of weather issues that make travel difficult or impossible (e.g., snow, rock slides, floods, fallen electrical lines, sinkholes, or rough seas). Many can lead to injuries or illness, or highlight other physical vulnerabilities. Food and water may be unavailable along the route. Roads, railway tracks, airport runways, or other infrastructure may be out of repair. Large animals, vehicles, or other objects may block one’s path.

Human Factors

Then there are the human-related components that will influence the outcome. We’ll find characters within travel comedies who are working against the protagonists. They are the people chasing, sabotaging, or misdirecting those we are rooting for. Or they are competitors in a race. Some are law enforcement personnel trying to put an end to the endeavor, even if for completely legitimate reasons. They could simply be other drivers or boaters who just happen to be in the way, or moving along in some fashion that significantly hinders the main characters.

We also have the protagonists inadvertently spoiling their own objectives. They will argue with one another and counter each other’s efforts. They will be ignorant of the direction to go or how to properly operate their vehicle. They will lack the money needed for essential supplies, including food, water, and fuel. They might have some physical or emotional shortcoming that makes reaching their destination problematic. They will travel too fast or too recklessly than what is safe for the conditions. Or they may interact with bystanders in such a way as to make them hostile.

Source: Eric Steinhauer / Pexels

The Audience Has Something to Say

These are the sorts of elements you will find in virtually all travel comedies. Each one draws the audience’s attention to vulnerabilities that must be overcome. The laughter directed at the protagonists is typically of the supportive, sympathetic, “lifting” sort as described by the Mutual Vulnerability Theory. Most of us have dealt with the same sorts of issues during our own travels, and we communicate a sense of shared frustration with the main characters. No matter how much danger they may be placed in, we know from past experience the central characters are never seriously hurt or killed. We can thus “distance” ourselves from the rage and cries of desperation that would otherwise engender feelings of distress rather than amusement.

The laughter we express toward antagonists, by comparison, tends to be of the “lowering” kind. We laugh “at” them because, while they may think they are capable of stopping the main characters from reaching the objective, in the end, they fail to do so. Thus, they have the same limitations as we do.

Consider this short YouTube clip from Tommy Boy starring Chris Farley and David Spade. Their car has already been mechanically compromised from hitting a deer (which miraculously survived unscathed), but the car’s hood release did not fare as well. What follows is a series of events that superbly highlights their emotional and physical vulnerabilities. Note how their mood goes from delightfully optimistic to terror in less than a second. Enjoy.

© John Charles Simon

item.title: How Trying the Opposite Can Help You Get Unstuck
item.description:
Relationships

How Trying the Opposite Can Help You Get Unstuck

When repeated solutions fail, changing your response can break the pattern.

Posted October 29, 2026

Key points
  • A useful 180-degree shift is a move that interrupts the usual pattern.
  • Repeating a solution that is not working can unintentionally maintain the problem you are trying to solve.
  • Changing even one response can disrupt a repetitive relationship pattern and change the outcome.

This post was co-authored by Jeffrey B. Jackson, Ph.D., LMFT, Associate Professor at Brigham Young University.

''We need a new way of thinking to solve the problems caused by the old way of thinking.'' — Einstein

A Gary Larson "Far Side" comic shows a boy pushing with all his might on a door to open it. A nearby sign reads “Midvale School for the Gifted.” And on the door, a single word: “Pull.”

No matter how smart we are, sometimes we end up managing things in our lives like this boy. When we encounter problems in our personal lives or our relationships, we do what we know how to do: We try harder. We explain more. We give more advice. We think harder. We try to control more. And the problem doesn’t budge. But what if the answer lies in changing direction rather than increasing our effort?

Interrupting Unhelpful Patterns

This idea of trying the opposite of what we’ve been doing comes from brief strategic therapy, an approach that examines how our attempted solutions may sometimes maintain or even worsen the problem we are trying to solve. The goal is to identify the pattern and respond in a way that interrupts it. Instead of trying harder, we may need to try something different. And trying the opposite can sometimes help us get unstuck.

Imagine a parent who is worried about some choices their teen is making. Reaching out with love and concern, the parent asks more questions. The teenager feels interrogated and shares less. The parent sees the teenager’s distance as proof that something is wrong and asks even more questions. Soon, the family is trapped in a loop: More worry leads to more pressure, more pressure leads to more withdrawal, and more withdrawal leads to more worry.

In other words, our efforts to solve a problem can sometimes keep it going—or even make it worse. A perfectly reasonable response can become unhelpful when we continue using it despite poor results.

The good news is that changing even one person’s response can often alter the pattern.

One way to break a stuck pattern is to ask a slightly odd question: What would be 180 degrees different from what I usually do?

This doesn’t mean doing the most extreme opposite thing imaginable. If someone tends to yell, the answer isn’t to become icy and silent for a week. A useful 180-degree turn is safe, respectful, and aimed at changing the specific pattern that is keeping you stuck.

Examples of Trying the Opposite in Everyday Life

  • If you keep pushing yourself to change through self-criticism, try accepting where you are right now a little more.
  • If you find yourself repeatedly lecturing a child, try listening more to better understand the child’s point of view.
  • If you tend to defend yourself when your partner criticizes you, try agreeing with the parts that might be true.
  • If you often rescue a loved one by taking over tasks they can manage, express confidence in that person’s abilities.
  • If you’re constantly arguing for change, become curious about the person’s reasons for not changing.
  • If you usually avoid having difficult conversations, try raising one specific concern.

Why can trying the opposite help? In relationships, a stuck pattern can develop in which each person’s response invites more of the very behavior they want to stop. Most people push back when they feel pressured or controlled—even when the other person means well. The more someone lectures, insists, or tries to force a decision, the more likely the other person is to argue, shut down, or dig in their heels. A better starting point is often to listen, remember that we can’t control anyone but ourselves, and avoid turning the conversation into a tug-of-war. A different response creates an opportunity for a different exchange.

Imagine your partner says to you, “You criticize everything I do.” You may quickly reply, “I do not—you’re the one being critical!” This response makes sense, but it can keep the argument going. Your partner hears another criticism, and now both of you become even more convinced that the other person is the problem. Instead of defending yourself, try agreeing with the parts that might be true. You might say, “I can see why it seems like I’m so critical. When I’m stressed, I can be quick to point out what I don’t like.” This doesn’t mean you’re admitting that you criticize everything or giving up your point of view. What it does do is stop the usual back-and-forth so you can both get back to the real issue.

When people feel heard and understood, they often become more open to another point of view; they no longer have to work so hard to convince someone that their experience makes sense or is valid.

Allowing Imperfection

The 180-degree-different strategy can also be useful when the struggle is with yourself. Imagine putting off a project because you are determined to get it right. You keep preparing, planning, and waiting to feel ready, but never begin. A 180-degree experiment might be to spend 10 minutes making a deliberately rough first attempt. Instead of trying to eliminate the possibility of imperfection before starting, you allow imperfection so you can start.

To implement the 180-degree change, you can:

  1. Notice the pattern. What do you repeatedly do to fix the problem? Explain? Defend? Check? Avoid? Control? Push? Rescue? Reassure? Then ask: Is it helping, or is it keeping the problem going?
  2. Try one new move. Try the opposite of what you’ve been doing, remembering that it can be a small change.
  3. Watch for changes. Give the experiment enough time to see whether the pattern shifts. Look for small signs of progress, not a total transformation overnight.

The central idea is simple: When a solution works, keep it. When it repeatedly fails, resist the urge to do it louder, longer, or harder. Try the opposite. This strategy is best suited to repetitive patterns that keep people stuck. Rather than needing to solve the whole problem, sometimes getting unstuck can start with changing the part that might be keeping the problem going.

item.title: Exploring Individualism and Collectivism
item.description:
Cross-Cultural Psychology

Exploring Individualism and Collectivism

Why one of psychology's most familiar ideas remains contested.

Posted October 29, 2026

Key points
  • Cultural differences are real, but often not straightforward.
  • Simple categories can obscure important real-world complexity.
  • A study of IBM employees shaped our view of national cultures.

Authored by Miles Thompson, Rachel Peal, and Ada Toprak.

You may have heard that Western cultures are individualistic and Eastern cultures are collectivist. So had we. So we set out to explore the research behind these ideas to see what it might teach us about our wider project, which is using psychology to help bring about a better world. In short, while the above distinction captures something real, we also came to understand that the underlying research is more complicated and nuanced than the simple statement above suggests.

The labels individualism and collectivism tend to be applied to whole countries or even global regions. By way of illustration, and using stereotypical examples, individualistic societies are generally associated with “the West” (e.g., the United States). They tend to have a greater emphasis on personal autonomy and individual goals, with individuals relying less on each other. Japan or China, on the other hand, are stereotypically used as exemplars of more collectivist societies. In these societies, individuals tend to be more interdependent, and group relationships and obligations are given greater importance.

Foundations

Individualism-collectivism research is often traced back to Geert Hofstede (1928-2020). Hofstede’s original work in the late 1960s and early 1970s used factor analysis to examine the results of a global survey of employee work values, conducted within IBM (International Business Machines). This research gathered data from mainly skilled, educated, middle-class employees working for a single multinational technology company in different locations around the world (Hofstede, 1980). This raises sampling questions, both in terms of who was sampled and the extent to which that data can represent national cultures.

Hofstede’s original framework included four dimensions of culture; later versions included six, of which individualism-collectivism is only one. Among the many items included in the survey, six came to be associated with the individualism-collectivism dimension. Here, participants were asked about factors they would like to see in an ideal job. The three individualism items focused on (i) having a job that allows time for personal and family life, (ii) having freedom within your job, and (iii) having challenging work resulting in a sense of accomplishment. The three collectivism items focused on having (i) training opportunities, (ii) good physical working conditions, and (iii) the scope for fully using your skills and abilities (Hofstede, 1980).

Potential issues

Naturally, researchers have noted that the above items appear much more narrowly focused than the overarching ideas of individualism and collectivism presented earlier. This raises questions of "face validity." In other words, do questionnaire items appear to measure what they claim to measure? There is also a related question concerning the leap from responses about workplace preferences and opportunities to conclusions about a national culture.

A large volume of research has since been produced on this topic. However, there is still no single, universally accepted definition or measurement of individualism and collectivism. Different studies approach the terms in different ways. Moreover, researchers disagree about how the two concepts relate to each other: Are they opposite ends of a single continuum, separate dimensions, or orientations that can coexist within the same person or society?

Researchers have long noted the difficulty of reducing the complexity of a national culture into one of two categories and/or a single continuum. Even mapping individualism-collectivism onto “East-West,” another problematic shorthand, raises questions. Making reductions like these (individualism-collectivism or East-West) risks treating different societies or regions, and the variations within them, as single, fixed units.

Moreover, even within a country, social and demographic variations such as gender, race, ethnicity, religion, generation, and political group membership may promote different values and ways of relating to each other. A country’s average score cannot, by itself, tell us how any particular individual thinks, feels, or behaves. Assuming that an individual shares the characteristics of their country's average is an example of something known as the "ecological fallacy."

These issues also matter when researchers use national individualism-collectivism scores to help explain other country-level outcomes, such as levels of well-being or social trust. Indeed, some researchers suggest that some of the potential issues above need to be carefully considered when interpreting research that explores these kinds of relationships (Oyserman et al., 2002; Voronov & Singer, 2002).

A recent example

To give an example of the complexity of researching this area, Lomas and colleagues (2023) explored a concept they thought would relate to individualism-collectivism: "self-care" versus "other-care." They analysed data from more than 120,000 people across 116 countries collected through the Gallup World Poll. The question asked was: “Do you think people should focus more on taking care of themselves or on taking care of others?”

Using the study’s own East-West groupings, and contrary to expectations that self-care would be more associated with individualism, respondents in “the East” put more importance on self-care than respondents in “the West.” The researchers wondered if (i) this might suggest that countries in the East are more individualistic than those in the West; (ii) self-care might not map onto individualism-collectivism; (iii) part of collectivism might include looking after yourself, as part of caring for the wider community; and (iv) self-care and other-care may carry different meanings in different cultural contexts.

As part of the same study, the researchers also asked about self-orientation versus other-orientation. Here, the data followed the researchers’ expected pattern: self-orientation was more common in the West than the East.

What the evidence does and does not support

The individualism-collectivism distinction is a helpful orienting framework. But after decades of research, the evidence does not justify treating individualism-collectivism as a simple, fixed property of whole countries, still less as a description of any one individual within it.

Many have argued that Hofstede's original individualism-collectivism work contains limitations. In response, researchers have revised, refined, and expanded the framework in different ways. Some are making substantial revisions to the original core variables; others are working to move beyond simple dichotomies, embracing more fluid, multidimensional dynamics; and others are more gently modifying the original dimension, using updated data and measures (Komisarof & Akaliyski, 2025; Uskul & Mesquita, 2026).

Countries do vary in terms of cultural values broadly captured by terms like individualism-collectivism. But how these terms are defined, measured, and relate to each other still seems to be up for debate. Moreover, focusing on individualism-collectivism alone risks overlooking other important cultural dimensions. The more we simplify and reduce, the more we seem to risk losing rather than gaining.

Equally, and notwithstanding all the above, one study examining 51 years of data from 78 countries found that individualistic practices and values had increased in most of the societies studied (Santos et al., 2017). That said, this does not mean that all societies are changing in the same way, nor that they are becoming culturally identical.

What could we conclude?

As measuring even simple aspects of individual human behaviour is complicated, measuring more nuanced aspects of national culture—like individualism-collectivism—is more challenging still, especially if our core definitions and the relationships between terms are not yet fully agreed upon. Without strong foundations, future conclusions risk not standing up to the test of time. This is potentially a wider issue in psychology, where attractive concepts become widely used before their assumptions and measurements are fully understood. Attractive categories help us begin thinking. But problems can arise when we mistake the map for the territory.
