item.title: Why Marriages Face Challenges During the Teen Years
item.description:
Marriage

Why Marriages Face Challenges During the Teen Years

Marital struggles during kids' teen years are not just about the teenagers.

Posted October 29, 2026

Key points
  • Marital satisfaction can decline when children reach adolescence, but teenagers are not necessarily the cause.
  • The adolescent years often concur with other tensions that can stress a marriage.
  • Understanding each partner's internal experience and the relationship dynamics can help couples become closer.
  • The first step in this process is self-reflection.
The unspoken distance between partners
Source: Sneksy/istock

Couples who are parents of teenagers often feel at their wits’ end. Irritated, isolated, even disillusioned, they may reflexively blame their teenager for the strain on their marriage. Sure, a teenager can test a marriage: Teenagers can be moody, engage in risky behaviors and expose differences in parenting styles. However, there often is much more to the story.

Let’s look more deeply at what each partner may be experiencing and the dynamics that may be unfolding between them. Here, I’m focusing on couples who are in their mid-40s to mid-50s and who have been together for about 15 years or longer.

Factor 1: Depletion

Life at this stage often comes with multiple concurrent demands. Imagine a couple, each closing in on 50 years old. They are at the peaks of their careers, with more responsibility, pressure and opportunity than ever. One lays awake at night, crunching the numbers for college tuition and retirement planning. On the weekends, they divide and conquer, not just with parenting tasks, but also with caring for aging parents. One experiences hot flashes and brain fog; the other is exhausted after the same workouts he’s done for years. Both have little left to give.

Factor 2: Reckoning

Alongside of the depletion, there can be a quieter internal process of reckoning. At this stage of life, the couple sees the results of their earlier life: what went well or poorly in parenting, finances, careers and relationships. While there is pride in the successes, there can also be the heavy feeling of regret. When their 16-year-old shuts the door again and again, one of them wonders, maybe we were too hard on him when he was little and are now paying the price.

There can also be growing awareness of the approaching empty nest, and with it, larger questions about life: What will life be like when my child leaves home? Will I have to confront my mortality more directly? What parts of my life do I want to carry forward and what parts would I like to leave behind? These thoughts may not be too loud; after all, there isn’t much time for existential questions. But the thoughts can begin to surface, leaving an unsettling feeling.

How This Strains a Relationship

Tired and bewildered, a couple may have less space for the relationship. Instead, their focus shrinks inward. This isn’t necessarily unhealthy. When we are depleted and overwhelmed, we may need to turn inward and care for and reconcile what’s inside. However, if we get stuck and do not move through our inner experiences well, our relationship can suffer.

In a struggling relationship, a couple may feel like they are living parallel lives, both headed in the same direction of launching teenagers but, in the meantime, their internal worlds are separate. Arguments arise over seemingly minor issues. One person attempts repair, the other rebuffs. It becomes too easy to slip into discord and too hard to stay connected.

Couples may see playfulness, presence and intimacy fade. Regret may lead to resentment, especially when those regrets are entangled in a partner’s past behaviors and personality. Unresolved resentment hardens distance into an impenetrable wall. Questions about the long-term sustainability of the relationship appear.

Clearly, this doesn’t happen in all relationships. And even when it does, it doesn’t reflect that there is something fundamentally wrong with the connection. Rather, there are considerable demands tied to the life stage and new feelings and questions that may not yet be understood.

In every challenge lies an opportunity. Here, as couples begin to understand their own experiences and their relational dynamics, they can find new ways to support one another.

Where to Begin

Start with yourself. In couples therapy, we sometimes zoom in on one partner’s experience before zooming back out to understand the couple with greater perspective. You can begin the same way, by taking a closer look at what is happening inside you. An inward gaze can help bring clarity about what you are experiencing and how to make it better.

Here are some prompts for self-reflection: What is happening inside me at this stage of my life? Is there something that I’m grieving, fearing, wanting or re-evaluating? How can I care for what is going on internally? How have I been feeling in my body, and how can I take care of my body well?

Consider journaling, since it may be a way for self-reflection to become an active, forward-moving process. If it’s too much to process on your own, consider an individual therapist or connecting with a good friend, not someone that will leave you feeling more disgruntled, but someone who can help you with your own understanding.

This may take a few passes. With so much going on both externally and internally, clarity may not happen overnight. However, creating a space for yourself is often the first step in moving through internal and relational discontent.

Use this as an opportunity to create a process that you can lean on both individually and as a couple to transform dissatisfaction into deeper connection.

I listed self-reflection as step 1. In this step, you are expanding your understanding of yourself and identifying how to advocate for yourself. In future posts, I will describe further steps which collectively provide a process you can turn to when you feel disconnect or tension rising in your relationship.

Each phase of life comes with its challenges. How we respond to them can have a big impact on our relationships and the chapters that follow. It’s worth learning to respond well.

To find a therapist, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: Could You Be in a "Silent Divorce"?
item.description:
Divorce

Could You Be in a "Silent Divorce"?

A few signs to help you assess if you may have fallen into a "silent divorce."

Posted October 29, 2026

Key points
  • The legal end of a marriage often begins many years before filing for a divorce.
  • Not every marriage ends with a flourish. Some just appear to fade away.
  • Even when there are signs that you might be in a "silent divorce", it does not mean your marriage is over.

As a matrimonial and family law attorney who regularly works alongside mental health professionals, I know that the legal end of a marriage usually begins many years before one of the partners ends up in my office filing for, or otherwise facing, a divorce.

In some cases, there are years of obvious distress in the marriage, in the form of resentment or infidelity, and sometimes even abuse. But in other cases, the marriage has deteriorated slowly, almost passively, in a quiet, and sometimes for one of the spouses, surprising way.

Not every marriage ends with a flourish. Some just appear to fade away.

Many call this a “silent divorce”. It occurs when a couple shares a home and a united front is presented to the outside world, but the relationship is no longer intimate or emotionally close. It is transactional, with most of the interactions revolving around children, logistics, family finances, and other more banal topics.

This allows for the couple to put on a happy façade for their family and community, but the deeper level of connection that likely once existed is no longer there.

Sometimes this arrangement lasts. Sometimes it does not. A lot of the time it is not even recognized. I have seen many arrive in my office after months or sometimes years of this behavior. And by the time they come to me, the separation has been happening for years.

Perhaps the hardest part is that a silent divorce is hard to spot even for those in one. Many believe they will simply “reconnect” when they “get out of the weeds” with children, aging parents, and building careers. But it is not always that easy.

Signs You Might Be Quietly Co-Existing in a Silent Divorce

1. Couple time is curtailed, or removed completely.

Instead of having meaningful interactions and occasional one-on-one date nights where you have a chance to truly reconnect, you and your spouse no longer desire to have that time together. You instead focus all of your interactions on external events you must attend together and child rearing if you have children together.

This is not the same as having a very busy life and not having the time to connect. In a silent divorce, the desire to connect on a deeper level is greatly reduced, or gone.

2. Communication is transactional.

Instead of having a true curiosity about the other person’s life, conversations become almost exclusively functional. The topics you discuss revolve around logistics and the day-to-day, from raising children to bill paying to household issues.

You might stop arguing, too, which is an interesting byproduct of a silent divorce. Not having hard conversations is not a good thing, as it sometimes signals a lack of interest in the relationship, or even resignation.

3. You live parallel lives.

This can creep up over time, but is one of the clearest signs that you are in this kind of arrangement, whether you planned it or not.

You have your own life, interests and friends, separate from your spouse. You live together and spend time together when necessary, but one or both partners turn to other friends, new hobbies, or even electronic means to find the emotional fulfillment and kinship missing from their marriage.

It is very possible to have separate interests and a very healthy marriage. But this component in a silent divorce does not include the part of the marriage that includes you keeping a close connection.

What Comes Next

Not every silent divorce ends with a legal filing or a visit to my or another attorney’s office.

Sometimes recognizing these behaviors in yourself and your partner can serve as a wake-up call. If you are willing to take steps to rebuild your emotional connection, you might want to enlist the help of a therapist to get back on the right path. The important issue is that both partners are willing to work at rebuilding.

Before deciding that this is you, here are a few questions you can ask yourself:

Have I been clear that I am unhappy to my partner? Is my partner also willing to work on this? Or are one or both of us more comfortable now as roommates rather than partners?

Divorce is a huge endeavor, so before you do anything rash, acknowledge what is happening and decide what to do. Silence can help you keep up appearances as an intact family, but it will not sustain a healthy, giving relationship.

And, as I always say, please take time to take care of yourself and your children through this very stressful time.
